stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Early sea charts badly distorted distances near the poles. Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish mapmaker who worked in the sixteenth ______ a projection that let sailors draw a constant compass bearing as a straight line. Navigators still rely on his map today.
explanation: The comma after "Mercator" opens an extra description: "a Flemish mapmaker who worked in the sixteenth century." You have to close it with the same mark, a comma, before the sentence returns to its subject. Cross the phrase out and you get "Gerardus Mercator designed a projection," which is a complete sentence. This is the basic move behind every SAT Boundaries question with a long interrupter: find the opening mark and match it at the close.

A.why: You left the interrupter open. A comma opened it after "Mercator," and nothing closes it, so the description runs straight into the verb "designed."

C.why: You added "and," which makes it look like two actions are being joined. But Mercator has no earlier verb for "designed" to pair with, so the sentence never gets a main verb.

D.why: You closed the interrupter with a dash when a comma opened it. The marks around an interruption have to match: comma with comma, dash with dash.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The minimum wage—a legal floor on hourly pay that most countries now ______ been debated by economists for more than a century. Critics argue that it reduces hiring in low-wage industries, while supporters point to studies finding little effect on overall employment.
explanation: A dash after "wage" opens the interruption, so you close it with a second dash. Remove the fenced-off part and you get "The minimum wage has been debated by economists," which is a complete sentence. Matching paired dashes shows up on the SAT whenever a dash opens far back in the sentence.

A.why: You closed with a comma when a dash opened the interruption. The marks have to match at both ends, so a dash needs a dash.

B.why: You left the interruption open. Without a closing dash, "most countries now enforce" runs straight into "has been debated," and the reader can't tell where the extra information ends.

D.why: You added "and," which makes it look like two verbs are being joined. But "the minimum wage" has no earlier verb, so "and has been" leaves the sentence without its main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most immune cells that fight an infection die off within weeks. Memory B cells, long-lived cells that form after an infection or a ______ able to recognize the same pathogen for years. This lasting recognition is a large part of what makes vaccines effective.
explanation: The comma after "Memory B cells" opens a description of what they are. You close that description with a matching comma before the verb "remain." Cross it out and you get "Memory B cells remain able to recognize the same pathogen," which is complete and correct. This is the core step for SAT items that bury the main verb behind an appositive.

A.why: You left the interrupter unclosed. The comma after "cells" opens the description, and with no closing comma it runs straight into "remain."

B.why: You used a semicolon, which goes only between two complete sentences. "Memory B cells, long-lived cells... vaccination" is not a complete sentence, and a semicolon also doesn't match the opening comma.

D.why: You added "and," which makes it look like two actions are being joined. But "Memory B cells" has no earlier verb, so the sentence ends up with no main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Bare fields lose topsoil quickly to winter rain and wind. Cover crops, plants such as rye or clover that farmers ______ the soil in place until spring planting. Their roots also add organic matter that later crops can use.
explanation: The comma after "Cover crops" opens a description that ends at "harvests." You close it with one comma there and add no commas inside it. Remove the description and you get "Cover crops hold the soil in place," which is a complete sentence. On SAT items like this, the wrong choices often scatter commas through the phrase. The fix is still one opening mark and one matching closing mark.

A.why: You added commas inside the phrase. They set off "between harvests" as if it were its own interruption, which leaves the outer description that started after "Cover crops" with no proper close.

C.why: You left the interrupter unclosed. Without a comma after "harvests," the description runs straight into the main verb "hold."

D.why: You put the comma inside the phrase, after "sow," instead of at its end. This breaks up "farmers sow between harvests" and still leaves the description unclosed before "hold."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Few animals on Earth travel as far as the arctic tern. This small seabird, which weighs only about 100 grams______ flies roughly 70,000 kilometers each year, following the summer from its Arctic breeding grounds to the waters off Antarctica and back again.
explanation: A comma after "seabird" opens the extra description "which weighs only about 100 grams." Extra information that opens with a comma must also close with a comma. That closing comma hands the sentence back to its main verb, "flies." Test it by crossing out the description: "This small seabird flies roughly 70,000 kilometers each year" is a complete, correct sentence. This is the one skill behind the SAT question type where an interruption opens long before the blank and you have to remember to close it.

A.why: You left the interruption open. The comma after "seabird" started the description, but nothing ends it. As written, "100 grams flies" runs together, and the reader can't tell where the description stops and the main verb starts.

B.why: You closed the interruption with a different mark from the one that opened it. It opened with a comma, so it has to close with a comma. A dash can close an interruption only if a dash opened it.

D.why: You added "and" as though the sentence joined two things the seabird does. But "weighs" sits inside the description, not beside "flies" as a second action. Adding "and" leaves the description unclosed and gives "flies" no proper link to its subject, "This small seabird."
